title: "Pipeline"
description: "An ordered sequence of data or model-processing steps that transforms inputs into useful outputs."
term: "Pipeline"
letter: "P"

difficulty: "Beginner"

## Simple explanation

A pipeline is a repeatable sequence of steps. In an AI system, data might be
validated, cleaned, transformed, passed to a model, and then turned into a
prediction or report.

## Technical explanation

A pipeline composes operations into a defined workflow, often with explicit
inputs, outputs, dependencies, and failure handling. A pipeline can run in
memory for model training or span distributed services and scheduled jobs
for data preparation and inference.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Explicit pipelines make preprocessing consistent between training and
inference, support reproducibility, and make failures easier to locate.
Production pipelines also expose operational concerns such as retries,
latency, monitoring, and data lineage.

## How it works

Each stage consumes an input, performs a bounded transformation, and passes
its output to a downstream stage. Implementations may run stages
sequentially, in parallel, or as a dependency graph. Reliable pipelines
validate stage contracts and make retries safe where possible.

## Practical example

An inference pipeline could check a request's schema, normalize text,
generate an embedding, retrieve relevant passages, call a language model,
and validate the response before returning it.

## Common misconceptions

- A pipeline is not necessarily a simple linear chain; stages may branch or
  run concurrently.
- Putting steps in a pipeline does not by itself make them reproducible:
  inputs, versions, configuration, and random seeds may also need tracking.
